title: Playing the blues on the way back from funerals; Buddy Petit's funeral
summary: Funeral practice, 'putting them in the alley', and the get-together band for Buddy Petit's funeral paid by a speakeasy owner.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: We were talking about those brass bands. You were saying Chris would get together, some of those guys?

Well yeah, bands like Renee and Chris, I mean our leaders like Renee and Chris, well they'd get a band, well then they would play this rough stuff like we do today, going and coming back to him to go to pick up the body, and what we call put them in the alley coming back. Put them in the alley? What does that mean? It's the blues. You know what I mean. I know what you mean.
I'm telling you the blues.
And I want you to tell me. The blues, man. But why did you call it put them in the alley? Well I just, I found it going on in the back.
I was at the gutter to pick up the body, and what we call put them in the alley coming back.
I guess you might wake up in the alley sometimes.
Well I haven't so far. You never woke up and didn't know where you're at?
I never did get that much. No.
Well say a funeral like Buddy Petit's funeral, who would play that?
I had a get together band, and Eureka played two bands. Louis Armstrong was part there. That's the time he was here at the Suburban Garden.
Do you remember who you had in your band?

All I could remember now, for sure, I know Jim was there, Big Jim, Robinson, and Edgar Mosley, the drum. That's but all I could remember. It's been such a long time ago. Well who paid you for that? Well we had the speakeasy at that time. You know what I mean by speakeasy. Well they had speakeasy, and the guy that operated the speakeasy, he paid for it. Because we left from his place, and we came back to his place, and brought the crowd.
Well he might have made money on that deal. Well he did. Was he a friend of Buddy's or something? No he was a friend of mine. He put up the money, huh? Oh yeah.
I used to play a lot of dancing for him at Poisevere and Hall of Economy, Incorporated, and so forth. What was his name? Ernest Delaro. He died some time back in Chicago.
Does his family play music any of them? No he wasn't a musician.
He just operated his business.
I thought I knew some Delaroes that played music.
Yeah, the brothers that have the shoemaker shop on Claver. That's right. Played saxophone clarinet.
See? How many people came to Buddy's funeral?
Well I don't know. It was something like the funeral was something on the order of Bicu you might say. Not quite as many, but he was well known.
Well did you know a guy named Hamp Vinson?
Hamp Vinson, yeah. That was the guy I was trying to call about in Chicago, Hamp Vinson. He the one who played trombone some time with us over there.
Yeah, that's the fella.
I couldn't think of the name. Yeah. Yeah, Hamp Vinson.
